newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine vote could hurt Russia debt talks - diplomat.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine vote could hurt Russia debt talks - diplomat.

text.p: A vote by parliament in Ukraine on Wednesday delaying approval of a deal renouncing its share of Soviet assets could hurt Russia's debt restructuring process, a Western diplomat said.

"This could prove a hiccup in those talks because they have been proceeding on the basis that everything is settled between Russia and the rest of the former Soviet Union," the diplomat, who asked not to be named, said.
The Russian government said earlier that the debt deal would stand despite the Kiev vote.
"This will have no impact on our relations with the Paris or London Clubs," Deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov told Reuters.

Russia has taken on responsibility for Soviet debt and won deals restructuring around $40 billion over 25 years with the Paris Club of government creditors, and about $35 billion for up to 25 years with the London Club of commercial bank creditors.
But the deals have not yet been formally closed and last-minute doubts about who is responsible for the debt could throw the process into confusion.

In December 1994, Ukrainian Prime Minister Vitaly Mosol and his Russian counterpart Viktor Chernomyrdin signed a "zero option deal" under which Kiev agreed to renounce claims to Soviet assets in exchange for Russia taking on all Soviet debts.

Ukraine is the only Commonwealth of Independent States member which has failed to ratify such a deal as nationalist deputies in parliament refuse to give up what they say is their share of gold, diamonds and other assets.

Deputies, feeling they have been sold out by the former leadership and sold short by Moscow, voted not to ratify the deal unless Russia reimbursed it for what it says is its 16.37 percent share of Soviet assets in gold and diamonds.
They also claimed about $700 million from frozen hard currency accounts held by the Vneshekonombank which was set up in the Soviet era.
"I'm not sure if Ukraine just wants more leverage or really means what it says. I'm not sure they've thought through the implications," the diplomat said.
"The Russians will certainly portray them as being unreliable and reneging on deals," he added.
Ukraine is itself considering enlisting the help of foreign banks and institutions to reschedule its debt to Russia, mostly for energy, of about $3.5 billion.
It is also planning to issue foreign bonds to help cover its 1997 budget deficit, but for that it would need a decent credit rating from Western institutions.
If Ukraine succeeded in assuming a large share of former Soviet debts, its creditworthiness would be affected. -- Kiev newsroom +38 044-229-2264
